facc-w1-q1.question: Ravi takes ₹5,000 from his cycle repair shop's cash box to buy groceries for his home. Which concept says this must be recorded as drawings, not as a business expense?
facc-w1-q1.explanation: The business entity concept treats the business and its owner as separate, so the owner's personal spending is drawings (equity falls), not an expense. Accrual only tells you when to record something, not whose spending it is.

facc-w1-q2.question: A business has total assets of ₹8,00,000 and total liabilities of ₹3,50,000. What is the owner's equity?
facc-w1-q2.explanation: Equity = Assets − Liabilities = 8,00,000 − 3,50,000 = ₹4,50,000. ₹11,50,000 comes from adding liabilities to assets — liabilities are outsiders' claims and must be subtracted.

facc-w1-q3.question: A consulting firm's financial year ends on 31 March. In March it delivered services worth ₹60,000, to be paid in April. Also in March it received a ₹10,000 advance for work to be done in April. Under the accrual concept, what is this year's (up to March) revenue?
facc-w1-q3.explanation: Revenue is recorded when earned: the ₹60,000 of services delivered in March is this year's revenue even though the cash comes later. The work for the ₹10,000 advance has not been done, so it is a liability. ₹70,000 comes from treating the advance as revenue too.

facc-w1-q4.question: At year-end a shop holds two items. Item X: cost ₹1,20,000, NRV ₹1,05,000. Item Y: cost ₹50,000, NRV ₹70,000. Apply the lower of cost and NRV rule item by item. What inventory figure appears in the balance sheet?
facc-w1-q4.explanation: Take the lower value for each item: X = min(1,20,000, 1,05,000) = 1,05,000; Y = min(50,000, 70,000) = 50,000. Total = ₹1,55,000. ₹1,70,000 comes from comparing total cost (1,70,000) with total NRV (1,75,000) — that hides X's ₹15,000 loss behind Y's gain.

facc-w1-q5.question: A factory machine would fetch only ₹40,000 as scrap today, but the balance sheet shows it at ₹3,00,000 (cost minus depreciation). Which assumption makes this correct?
facc-w1-q5.explanation: Going concern assumes the business will continue and keep using the machine, so it is shown at cost minus depreciation, not scrap value. Conservatism is the tempting trap, but it deals with uncertain losses — it does not mean writing a working machine down to scrap value.

facc-w1-q6.question: A business starts with Assets of ₹5,00,000 and Liabilities of ₹2,00,000. Then: (i) it pays creditors ₹40,000 in cash, (ii) it provides services worth ₹70,000 on credit, (iii) it pays rent of ₹15,000 in cash, (iv) the owner withdraws ₹10,000 for personal use. What is equity at the end?
facc-w1-q6.explanation: Opening equity = 5,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 3,00,000. Revenue +70,000, rent −15,000, drawings −10,000 ⇒ ₹3,45,000. Paying creditors cuts cash and liabilities by 40,000 each and leaves equity unchanged. ₹3,05,000 is the trap of also taking that 40,000 off equity; ₹3,55,000 comes from forgetting drawings. Check: assets 5,05,000 = liabilities 1,60,000 + equity 3,45,000.

facc-w1-q7.question: For the last 5 years a company charged depreciation on its machines using the straight line method. This year, with no valid reason, it switched to the WDV method just so that profit would look different. Which concept was broken?
facc-w1-q7.explanation: Consistency says that once a method is chosen it must be used every year so the years can be compared; a change is allowed only for a valid reason and with disclosure in the notes. Going concern is the trap because it is linked to depreciation, but it only assumes the business will keep running — it says nothing about switching methods.

facc-w1-q8.question: 'Kaveri Bakes' bought land for a shop in 2018 for ₹12,00,000. Today its market value is ₹30,00,000. Under the basic historical cost rule, at what amount will the land appear in the balance sheet?
facc-w1-q8.explanation: Historical cost concept: an asset is recorded at the cost paid when it was bought, not at today's market value (and land is not depreciated). ₹30,00,000 is the market value, ₹18,00,000 is only the rise in value, and ₹42,00,000 wrongly adds the two together.

facc-w1-q9.question: A company believes it will win a court case and receive ₹3,00,000 next year, but the verdict has not come yet. Under conservatism (prudence), what should it do this year?
options: Record half, that is ₹1,50,000, as income now
Record a ₹3,00,000 asset and an equal liability now
Record no income now; record it once it is certain
facc-w1-q9.explanation: Prudence: recognise expected losses early, but do not record gains until they are certain. The case has not been won yet, so there is no income. 'Record half' looks like a compromise, but no part of an uncertain gain becomes income yet.

facc-w1-q10.question: A business bought a ₹60,000 machine: it paid ₹20,000 in cash and owes the rest to the supplier. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets +₹60,000, Liabilities +₹60,000, no effect on Equity
Assets +₹40,000, Equity +₹40,000, no effect on Liabilities
Assets +₹40,000, Liabilities +₹40,000, no effect on Equity
facc-w1-q10.explanation: Machine +60,000 and cash −20,000, so net assets +40,000. The 40,000 still owed to the supplier is a liability. There is no income or expense, so equity is unchanged. 'Assets +₹60,000' forgets the fall in cash, and raising equity is wrong because buying a machine is not profit.

facc-w1-q11.question: In March a trader sold goods costing ₹1,00,000 for ₹1,50,000 on credit; the customer will pay in April. The salesman's 5% commission (on sale value) for this sale will be paid in April. The financial year ends on 31 March. Under accrual and matching, what is the profit from this sale up to March?
facc-w1-q11.explanation: Revenue was earned in March: 1,50,000. Matching puts that sale's expenses in March too: cost 1,00,000 + commission 1,50,000 × 5% = 7,500. Profit = ₹42,500. ₹50,000 treats the commission as April's (cash timing), ₹0 is cash-basis thinking, and ₹45,000 comes from applying the commission to cost.

facc-w1-q12.question: At the start a business has Assets ₹3,00,000 = Liabilities ₹1,00,000 + Equity ₹2,00,000. Then: (i) the owner brings in ₹50,000 more capital in cash, (ii) goods worth ₹30,000 are bought on credit, (iii) goods costing ₹20,000 are sold for ₹28,000 on credit, (iv) ₹12,000 of bank loan principal is repaid, (v) ₹5,000 interest is paid in cash. What are total assets and equity at the end?
facc-w1-q12.explanation: Assets: 3,00,000 + 50,000 + 30,000 + (28,000 − 20,000) − 12,000 − 5,000 = 3,71,000. Liabilities: 1,00,000 + 30,000 − 12,000 = 1,18,000. Equity: 2,00,000 + 50,000 + 8,000 (profit on sale) − 5,000 = ₹2,53,000; check 1,18,000 + 2,53,000 = 3,71,000. ₹2,41,000 is the trap of treating principal as an expense; ₹3,91,000 / ₹2,73,000 does not remove the sold goods from inventory; ₹3,21,000 forgets the new capital.

facc-w1-q13.question: A proprietor's business has this data for the year: cash sales ₹4,00,000; at year end ₹50,000 of credit sales is still due from customers; expenses paid in cash ₹2,20,000, which include ₹30,000 for the owner's home electricity bill; ₹15,000 of the year's rent is still unpaid. Using the accrual and business entity concepts, what is the business's profit?
facc-w1-q13.explanation: Revenue = 4,00,000 + 50,000 = 4,50,000 (credit sales are earned too). Expenses = 2,20,000 − 30,000 (the home bill is drawings) + 15,000 (outstanding rent) = 2,05,000. Profit = ₹2,45,000. ₹1,80,000 is plain cash basis; ₹2,15,000 treats the owner's bill as a business expense; ₹2,60,000 forgets the unpaid rent.

facc-w1-q14.question: At year end a shop has three items. A: cost ₹80,000, NRV ₹95,000. B: cost ₹60,000, NRV ₹42,000. C: cost ₹40,000, NRV ₹36,000. Apply lower of cost and NRV item by item. What inventory will be shown, and how much lower is profit than if everything were shown at cost?
facc-w1-q14.explanation: Item by item: A = 80,000 (cost is lower), B = 42,000, C = 36,000 ⇒ ₹1,58,000. Total cost was 1,80,000, so the write-down is 22,000 (18,000 on B + 4,000 on C), and profit falls by that much. ₹1,73,000 is total NRV — the aggregate comparison hides the losses on B and C behind A's gain; ₹1,62,000 adjusts only B.

facc-w1-q15.question: A business has opening Assets ₹5,00,000 and Liabilities ₹1,50,000. During the year: (i) the owner gave her personal car (value ₹2,00,000) to the business as capital, (ii) her child's school fee of ₹25,000 was paid from the business account, (iii) a ₹40,000 service was provided for cash, (iv) ₹18,000 of staff salary is outstanding. What are the year's profit and the closing equity?
facc-w1-q15.explanation: Profit = service 40,000 − outstanding salary 18,000 = ₹22,000. Equity = 3,50,000 (opening) + 2,00,000 (car as capital) − 25,000 (drawings) + 22,000 = ₹5,47,000. The car is capital and the school fee is drawings — both change equity but not profit. −₹3,000 treats the fee as an expense, ₹2,22,000 treats the car as income, and ₹40,000 / ₹5,65,000 forgets the outstanding salary.

facc-w2-q1.question: Which of these items is this month's **expense**, not an asset?
facc-w2-q1.explanation: This month's electricity has been used up this month and gives no future benefit, so it is an expense. Machinery and the patent will serve for several years (capital expenditure), and inventory will be sold later — all three are assets.

facc-w2-q2.question: Which statement about the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss is correct?
options: The balance sheet shows the position on a date; the P&L shows performance over a period
The balance sheet shows performance over a period; the P&L shows the position on a date
Both show the position on the same date, only the format differs
Assets and liabilities appear in the P&L, revenue in the balance sheet
facc-w2-q2.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot 'as at 31 March' — what is owned and owed on that day. The P&L covers 'the year ended 31 March' — what was earned and spent across the whole year. The second option is the reverse and is the most common confusion.

facc-w2-q3.question: A trading firm's items for the year: revenue ₹9,00,000; cost of goods sold ₹5,40,000; salaries ₹1,20,000; rent ₹60,000; purchase of a new delivery van ₹3,00,000; depreciation on the van ₹30,000; repayment of bank loan principal ₹50,000; loan interest ₹10,000. What is the profit for the year?
facc-w2-q3.explanation: Subtract only expenses: 9,00,000 − 5,40,000 − 1,20,000 − 60,000 − 30,000 − 10,000 = ₹1,40,000. The van purchase is capital expenditure (it becomes an asset; only depreciation goes to P&L) and principal repayment is not an expense. ₹90,000 comes from subtracting the repayment, −₹1,30,000 from expensing the van, ₹1,70,000 from forgetting depreciation.

facc-w2-q4.question: A company has total assets of ₹12,00,000. Current liabilities are ₹2,20,000, non-current liabilities ₹3,00,000 and share capital ₹5,00,000. What are reserves and surplus?
facc-w2-q4.explanation: Total equity = 12,00,000 − 2,20,000 − 3,00,000 = 6,80,000. Share capital is 5,00,000 of that, so reserves = ₹1,80,000. ₹6,80,000 is the whole of equity (share capital not removed), and ₹4,80,000 / ₹4,00,000 come from leaving out one type of liability.

facc-w2-q5.question: A bakery sells its old oven for ₹85,000. On the day of sale the oven's carrying amount (cost − depreciation) was ₹70,000. What appears in the statement of profit and loss?
options: Nothing, only the balance sheet changes
facc-w2-q5.explanation: Selling an oven is not the bakery's normal business, so the full ₹85,000 is not revenue. Only the gain = 85,000 − 70,000 = ₹15,000 (other income) goes to P&L. The sale price exceeds the carrying amount, so it is not a loss.

facc-w2-q6.question: A proprietor's opening equity was ₹4,00,000. During the year she introduced ₹1,00,000 of extra capital and made drawings of ₹30,000. Closing equity is ₹5,20,000. What was the profit for the year?
facc-w2-q6.explanation: Closing = Opening + capital introduced + profit − drawings ⇒ 5,20,000 = 4,00,000 + 1,00,000 + P − 30,000 ⇒ P = ₹50,000. ₹1,20,000 is just the change in equity (new capital is not profit); ₹20,000 comes from forgetting to add drawings back; ₹1,50,000 from forgetting to remove the new capital.

facc-w2-q7.question: Which of these items is a **liability** of the business on 31 March?
options: An advance received from a customer whose goods are still to be delivered
Staff salary to be paid next year
facc-w2-q7.explanation: Taking the advance created a present obligation to deliver goods, so it is a liability. Receivables and inventory are assets. Next year's salary is a future cost — the work has not been done yet, so there is no obligation today; this is the most common trap.

facc-w2-q8.question: Which of these costs of a packaging unit is **capital expenditure**?
options: Buying a new packing machine for the factory
Routine servicing of an old machine
facc-w2-q8.explanation: A new machine gives benefits for several years, so it becomes an asset and is expensed each year as depreciation. Rent, salary and routine servicing are day-to-day costs (revenue expenditure) — servicing is linked to a machine but does not create a new asset.

facc-w2-q9.question: A salon's service revenue for the year is ₹6,40,000, and it made a gain of ₹10,000 on selling an old chair. Expenses for the year are ₹4,70,000. What is the profit?
facc-w2-q9.explanation: Income includes both revenue and gains: 6,40,000 + 10,000 = 6,50,000. Profit = 6,50,000 − 4,70,000 = ₹1,80,000. ₹1,70,000 leaves out the gain, ₹1,60,000 subtracts the gain, and ₹11,20,000 adds the expenses.

facc-w2-q10.question: Year-end items of a trading business: cash ₹70,000; inventory ₹1,10,000; trade receivables ₹60,000; furniture ₹90,000; trade payables ₹80,000; bank loan ₹1,00,000; advance received from a customer ₹20,000. What is the owner's equity?
facc-w2-q10.explanation: Assets = 70,000 + 1,10,000 + 60,000 + 90,000 = 3,30,000. Liabilities = 80,000 + 1,00,000 + 20,000 = 2,00,000. Equity = ₹1,30,000. ₹1,50,000 does not treat the advance as a liability, ₹1,70,000 turns it into an asset, and ₹2,30,000 forgets the bank loan.

facc-w2-q11.question: A shop's items for the year: sales ₹7,50,000; cost of goods sold ₹4,20,000; rent ₹60,000; owner's drawings ₹50,000; purchase of new machinery ₹1,00,000; depreciation on machinery ₹20,000; loan interest ₹15,000. What is the profit for the year?
facc-w2-q11.explanation: Subtract only expenses: 7,50,000 − 4,20,000 − 60,000 − 20,000 − 15,000 = ₹2,35,000. Drawings are not an expense (the ₹1,85,000 trap), the machinery purchase is capital expenditure (the ₹1,35,000 trap), and forgetting depreciation gives ₹2,55,000.

facc-w2-q12.question: Some years ago a printing firm bought a machine for ₹2,40,000; accumulated depreciation so far is ₹1,50,000. The machine was sold for ₹70,000 in cash. Before this sale the year's profit was ₹3,00,000. What is the effect of the sale in the P&L, and what is the final profit?
facc-w2-q12.explanation: Carrying amount = 2,40,000 − 1,50,000 = 90,000. The sale price of 70,000 is below carrying amount, so loss = ₹20,000; profit = 3,00,000 − 20,000 = ₹2,80,000. A ₹70,000 gain treats the whole sale value as income, 'gain ₹20,000' flips the sign, and a ₹1,70,000 loss ignores depreciation and compares with original cost.

facc-w2-q13.question: A company had opening share capital of ₹10,00,000 and reserves and surplus of ₹3,00,000. During the year it issued new shares worth ₹2,00,000 at face value. Closing total assets are ₹22,00,000 and total liabilities ₹5,50,000. No dividend was paid during the year. What was the year's profit?
facc-w2-q13.explanation: Closing equity = 22,00,000 − 5,50,000 = 16,50,000. Share capital is now 12,00,000, so closing reserves = 4,50,000. Profit = 4,50,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹1,50,000. ₹3,50,000 is the whole change in equity (new shares are not profit), ₹4,50,000 is the closing reserves, and ₹6,50,000 forgets to subtract the new shares.

facc-w2-q14.question: A proprietor's year-end items: cash ₹50,000; advance received from a customer ₹30,000; patent ₹80,000; outstanding salary ₹25,000; trade receivables ₹70,000; bank loan ₹1,20,000; equipment ₹1,75,000. Capital at the start of the year was ₹1,50,000, no new capital came in during the year, and drawings were ₹40,000. What was the year's profit?
facc-w2-q14.explanation: Assets = 50,000 + 80,000 + 70,000 + 1,75,000 = 3,75,000. Liabilities = 30,000 + 25,000 + 1,20,000 = 1,75,000. Equity = 2,00,000 = 1,50,000 + profit − 40,000 ⇒ profit = ₹90,000. ₹1,50,000 treats the advance as an asset, ₹50,000 forgets drawings, and ₹10,000 subtracts drawings instead of adding them back.

facc-w2-q15.question: A proprietor's opening equity was ₹6,00,000. During the year: revenue ₹9,00,000; expenses ₹7,20,000; gain on selling an old van ₹15,000; a ₹1,00,000 bank loan taken and ₹50,000 repaid; drawings ₹60,000. What is the closing equity?
facc-w2-q15.explanation: Profit = 9,00,000 − 7,20,000 + 15,000 = 1,95,000. Closing equity = 6,00,000 + 1,95,000 − 60,000 = ₹7,35,000. Taking or repaying a loan only changes cash and liabilities, not equity — adding the net ₹50,000 gives ₹7,85,000. ₹7,20,000 forgets the gain and ₹7,95,000 forgets drawings.

facc-w3-q1.question: Before 31 March a magazine publisher receives ₹1,20,000 of subscriptions for issues to be sent next year. In the 31 March balance sheet, what is this amount?
facc-w3-q1.explanation: The cash has come in but the obligation to deliver the magazines remains, so it is unearned revenue — a liability. Treating it as this year's revenue is the most common trap; revenue arises as the issues are sent.

facc-w3-q2.question: Staff worked in March; their ₹40,000 salary will be paid in April. The financial year ends on 31 March. What is the correct treatment?
options: A ₹40,000 expense in March, and a ₹40,000 liability on 31 March
An April expense, because the cash goes out in April
No entry until it is paid
facc-w3-q2.explanation: Accrual concept: the expense arises when the service is used — in March. It has not been paid yet, so an outstanding salary liability also arises. 'An April expense' is cash-basis thinking.

facc-w3-q3.question: On 1 January 2026 a shop paid ₹1,20,000 in advance as rent for a full 12 months. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. What is prepaid rent in the 31 March 2026 balance sheet?
facc-w3-q3.explanation: Jan–Mar = 3 months belong to this year: expense = 1,20,000 × 3/12 = 30,000. The benefit of the other 9 months comes later: prepaid = 1,20,000 × 9/12 = ₹90,000. ₹30,000 is this year's expense, not the prepayment — the trap is swapping the two.

facc-w3-q4.question: On 1 August 2025 an online learning startup received ₹24,000 from a customer for a 12-month subscription. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. How much revenue is recognised in this financial year?
facc-w3-q4.explanation: Service was provided for 8 months, Aug to Mar: 24,000 × 8/12 = ₹16,000. The remaining ₹8,000 is unearned revenue (a liability). ₹14,000 comes from counting 7 months; ₹24,000 is the trap of treating all the cash as revenue.

facc-w3-q5.question: A company forgot to record March's ₹12,000 electricity bill (to be paid in April). What is the effect on the 31 March statements?
options: Profit is overstated by ₹12,000 and liabilities understated by ₹12,000
Profit is understated by ₹12,000 and liabilities overstated by ₹12,000
Profit is correct, only cash is wrong
Profit is overstated by ₹12,000 and assets overstated by ₹12,000
facc-w3-q5.explanation: The missing entry is an expense of ₹12,000 and an outstanding liability of ₹12,000. Without the expense, profit (and equity) is ₹12,000 too high and liabilities ₹12,000 too low. Cash is unaffected because payment is in April — the 'only cash is wrong' option gets this backwards.

facc-w3-q6.question: During the year a firm collected ₹5,00,000 in cash from customers, of which ₹40,000 related to last year's sales. At year-end ₹60,000 from this year's sales is still receivable. It paid ₹3,20,000 in cash for expenses, of which ₹10,000 is prepaid for next year; and ₹25,000 of expenses are still outstanding. What is this year's profit on the accrual basis?
facc-w3-q6.explanation: Revenue = 5,00,000 − 40,000 (last year's) + 60,000 (receivable) = 5,20,000. Expenses = 3,20,000 − 10,000 (prepaid) + 25,000 (outstanding) = 3,35,000. Profit = ₹1,85,000. ₹1,80,000 is the cash-basis answer; ₹2,25,000 comes from not removing last year's ₹40,000; ₹1,65,000 from adding the prepayment instead of subtracting it.

facc-w3-q7.question: On 31 March a company has ₹18,000 of prepaid insurance (premium already paid for next year's months). What is this in the balance sheet?
facc-w3-q7.explanation: The money was paid first and the benefit (insurance cover) comes later, so prepaid is a current asset. Calling it a liability is the trap of swapping prepaid and unearned — it would be a liability only if we had received money and still owed something.

facc-w3-q8.question: A company's FD earned ₹6,000 of interest this year, but the bank has not yet credited it to the account. The financial year ends on 31 March. What is the correct treatment?
options: No entry until the bank credits it
facc-w3-q8.explanation: Accrued income: the interest was earned this year, so the income belongs to this year; the cash has not come in, so interest receivable is an asset. 'No entry' is cash-basis thinking, and a liability is wrong because the company is owed money, it does not owe it.

facc-w3-q9.question: On 1 December 2025 a firm paid a 12-month insurance premium of ₹24,000. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. What is this year's insurance expense?
facc-w3-q9.explanation: Dec, Jan, Feb, Mar = 4 months belong to this year: 24,000 × 4/12 = ₹8,000. The other ₹16,000 is a prepaid asset, not expense. ₹6,000 counts only 3 months, and ₹24,000 treats the whole payment as expense.

facc-w3-q10.question: Which of these year-end adjustments **reduces** profit?
options: Removing next year's prepaid rent from expense and making it an asset
Recording this year's accrued interest income
Moving the part of unearned revenue earned this year into revenue
facc-w3-q10.explanation: Outstanding wages add a new expense (and a liability), so profit falls. Removing prepaid from expense, recording accrued income, and moving the earned part of unearned revenue into revenue all increase profit. Pattern: accrued expenses and unearned revenue (until earned) keep profit lower.

facc-w3-q11.question: On 1 November 2025 a gym collected ₹6,000 per member in advance from 1,000 members for a 12-month membership. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. What unearned revenue will the balance sheet show on 31 March 2026?
facc-w3-q11.explanation: Total advance = 1,000 × 6,000 = 60,00,000. Service was given for Nov–Mar = 5 months: earned = 60,00,000 × 5/12 = 25,00,000. The remaining 7 months = ₹35,00,000 liability. ₹25,00,000 is this year's revenue (the swap trap), ₹60,00,000 treats nothing as earned, and ₹30,00,000 comes from miscounting the months.

facc-w3-q12.question: A firm (year end 31 March 2026) has an unadjusted profit of ₹3,50,000. Errors: (a) 12 months' rent of ₹48,000 paid on 1 September 2025 was fully expensed; (b) March wages of ₹22,000 were not recorded; (c) a 3-month consulting fee of ₹45,000 received in advance on 1 February 2026 was put fully into revenue; (d) the year's depreciation of ₹18,000 was not recorded. What is the adjusted profit?
facc-w3-q12.explanation: (a) Sep–Mar = 7 months: expense 28,000, prepaid 20,000 ⇒ +20,000. (b) −22,000. (c) Feb and Mar are earned = 30,000; April's 15,000 is unearned ⇒ −15,000. (d) −18,000. Total = 3,50,000 + 20,000 − 22,000 − 15,000 − 18,000 = ₹3,15,000. ₹3,19,000 counts 6 months of rent, ₹2,85,000 removes the whole advance, and ₹2,75,000 subtracts the prepaid instead of adding it.

facc-w3-q13.question: At year end the accountant missed two things: (i) did not record ₹15,000 of accrued interest income, and (ii) left ₹9,000 of prepaid insurance fully in expense. What is the combined effect on reported profit and total assets?
options: Profit overstated by ₹24,000 and assets overstated by ₹24,000
Profit understated by ₹6,000 and assets understated by ₹6,000
Profit understated by ₹24,000, no effect on assets
Profit understated by ₹24,000 and assets understated by ₹24,000
facc-w3-q13.explanation: (i) Both income and the receivable were missed: profit −15,000, assets −15,000. (ii) The prepaid asset was not created and expense stayed too high: profit −9,000, assets −9,000. Combined: both are ₹24,000 too low. ₹6,000 comes from treating the prepaid the other way round; 'no effect on assets' forgets that every adjustment also touches a balance sheet item.

facc-w3-q14.question: During the year a company paid ₹9,60,000 of salary in cash. This includes ₹70,000 of last year's outstanding salary paid this year. At year end, ₹85,000 of this year's salary is still outstanding. On an accrual basis, what is this year's salary expense?
facc-w3-q14.explanation: Expense = cash paid − last year's part + this year's unpaid part = 9,60,000 − 70,000 + 85,000 = ₹9,75,000. ₹9,45,000 flips both signs, ₹9,60,000 is plain cash basis, and ₹11,15,000 adds last year's 70,000 instead of subtracting it.

facc-w3-q15.question: A software firm received two subscription advances: ₹36,000 on 1 July 2025 (for 12 months) and ₹18,000 on 1 January 2026 (for 6 months). The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. What are this year's revenue and the unearned revenue on 31 March?
facc-w3-q15.explanation: First: Jul–Mar = 9 months ⇒ 36,000 × 9/12 = 27,000 earned, 9,000 unearned. Second: Jan–Mar = 3 of 6 months ⇒ 18,000 × 3/6 = 9,000 earned, 9,000 unearned. Total: revenue ₹36,000, unearned ₹18,000. ₹54,000 treats all cash as revenue; ₹33,000 counts 8 months for the first; ₹31,500 spreads the second over 12 months although it covers 6.

facc-w4-q1.question: Purchase prices rose steadily all year. Comparing FIFO with weighted average, which statement is correct?
options: Weighted average gives higher closing inventory and higher profit
Both methods always give the same profit
FIFO gives higher closing inventory and higher profit
FIFO gives higher COGS and lower profit
facc-w4-q1.explanation: Under FIFO the older, cheaper units go to COGS first and the newer, dearer units remain in closing inventory. So with rising prices FIFO gives lower COGS and higher profit. The last option would be true if prices were falling.

facc-w4-q2.question: Opening inventory 50 units @ ₹200, purchase 1: 150 units @ ₹220, purchase 2: 100 units @ ₹250. 220 units were sold in the period. What is the cost of goods sold under FIFO?
facc-w4-q2.explanation: FIFO: 50 × 200 = 10,000; 150 × 220 = 33,000; remaining 20 × 250 = 5,000 ⇒ COGS = ₹48,000 (closing = 80 × 250 = 20,000). ₹49,867 is weighted average (68,000 ÷ 300 × 220), ₹51,400 is LIFO (newest units first), which Ind AS does not allow, and ₹44,000 is the trap of costing every unit at ₹200.

facc-w4-q3.question: Opening 40 units @ ₹100 and a purchase of 60 units @ ₹110. 70 units are sold. What is the value of closing inventory under the weighted average (periodic) method?
facc-w4-q3.explanation: Average = (4,000 + 6,600) ÷ 100 = ₹106 per unit. Closing 30 units × 106 = ₹3,180. ₹3,150 comes from a simple average of the prices (105), ignoring the units; ₹3,300 is the FIFO answer and ₹3,000 the LIFO answer.

facc-w4-q4.question: A machine is bought for ₹5,00,000 with a useful life of 5 years and a residual value of ₹50,000. Under the straight line method, what is its carrying amount after 2 years?
facc-w4-q4.explanation: Annual depreciation = (5,00,000 − 50,000) ÷ 5 = 90,000. Two years give 1,80,000 ⇒ carrying amount = ₹3,20,000. ₹3,00,000 comes from ignoring the residual value (1,00,000 per year).

facc-w4-q5.question: A delivery van costing ₹5,00,000 is depreciated at 20% on the written-down value method. What is the depreciation for the third year?
facc-w4-q5.explanation: Year 1: 5,00,000 × 20% = 1,00,000 (leaving 4,00,000). Year 2: 4,00,000 × 20% = 80,000 (leaving 3,20,000). Year 3: 3,20,000 × 20% = ₹64,000. ₹1,00,000 is the trap of applying the rate to cost every year; ₹51,200 is year four.

facc-w4-q6.question: At year-end a company faces three court cases. Case A: ₹4,00,000, lawyers say losing is probable and the amount is reliable. Case B: ₹6,00,000, losing is only possible. Case C: ₹2,00,000, the chance of losing is remote. Under Ind AS 37, how much is recognised as a provision and how much is disclosed as a contingent liability?
facc-w4-q6.explanation: A is probable and measurable ⇒ a ₹4,00,000 provision (expense + liability). B is possible ⇒ ₹6,00,000 appears only in the notes as a contingent liability. C is remote ⇒ not even disclosed. Disclosing ₹8,00,000 is the trap of including the remote case; a ₹10,00,000 provision comes from treating possible as probable.

facc-w4-q7.question: A shop's opening inventory is ₹40,000, purchases for the year ₹2,10,000 and closing inventory ₹55,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
facc-w4-q7.explanation: COGS = opening + purchases − closing = 40,000 + 2,10,000 − 55,000 = ₹1,95,000. ₹2,25,000 swaps opening and closing, ₹1,55,000 forgets opening inventory, and ₹3,05,000 adds closing instead of subtracting it.

facc-w4-q8.question: Under Ind AS 2, which statement about costing interchangeable (identical) inventory items is correct?
options: LIFO and FIFO are allowed, weighted average is not
A simple average of purchase prices is the best method
LIFO is not allowed; FIFO or weighted average must be used
facc-w4-q8.explanation: For interchangeable items Ind AS 2 allows only FIFO or weighted average cost, not LIFO. Specific identification is for unique items (such as custom machinery). A simple average is wrong because it ignores the weight of units.

facc-w4-q9.question: On which of a company's assets is depreciation usually **not** charged?
facc-w4-q9.explanation: Land usually does not have a limited useful life, so it is usually not depreciated. A building, a van and computers wear out with time and use, so their cost is spread over their useful life. Treating building and land the same is a common trap.

facc-w4-q10.question: A studio bought a printer for ₹1,80,000; residual value is ₹20,000 and useful life 4 years. What is the yearly depreciation under the straight line method?
facc-w4-q10.explanation: Depreciable amount = 1,80,000 − 20,000 = 1,60,000; each year = 1,60,000 ÷ 4 = ₹40,000. ₹45,000 forgets to subtract the residual value, ₹50,000 adds it, and ₹1,60,000 puts the whole depreciable amount into one year.

facc-w4-q11.question: A customer has filed a ₹5,00,000 case against a company. The lawyers say losing is possible but not probable. Under Ind AS 37, what happens at year end?
options: No provision; disclose as a contingent liability in the notes
Nothing — no provision and no disclosure
A ₹2,50,000 provision and the rest disclosed in the notes
facc-w4-q11.explanation: The outflow is only possible, not probable, so no provision is made; but the chance is not remote either, so it is disclosed in the notes as a contingent liability. A full provision would be needed only if losing were probable; 'nothing' is only for a remote case; a half provision is not a rule.

facc-w4-q12.question: Opening inventory 200 units @ ₹30; purchase 1: 300 units @ ₹34; purchase 2: 250 units @ ₹38. During the period 600 units were sold at ₹50 per unit. Under FIFO, what are the gross profit and closing inventory?
facc-w4-q12.explanation: FIFO COGS = 200 × 30 + 300 × 34 + 100 × 38 = 6,000 + 10,200 + 3,800 = 20,000. Revenue = 600 × 50 = 30,000 ⇒ GP ₹10,000. Closing = 150 × 38 = ₹5,700. ₹8,800 / ₹4,500 sells the newest units first like LIFO (not allowed under Ind AS 2); ₹9,440 / ₹5,140 is weighted average (25,700 ÷ 750), not FIFO; ₹9,600 / ₹5,100 uses the simple average price of ₹34.

facc-w4-q13.question: A company is comparing two methods for an ₹8,00,000 machine. Option 1: SLM, residual value ₹80,000, life 6 years. Option 2: WDV at 25%. What is the total depreciation for the first 2 years under each method?
facc-w4-q13.explanation: SLM: (8,00,000 − 80,000) ÷ 6 = 1,20,000 a year ⇒ 2 years = ₹2,40,000. WDV: year 1 = 8,00,000 × 25% = 2,00,000; year 2 = 6,00,000 × 25% = 1,50,000 ⇒ ₹3,50,000. ₹2,66,667 forgets the residual under SLM; ₹4,00,000 applies the WDV rate to cost every year; ₹3,15,000 subtracts the residual first under WDV, which WDV does not do.

facc-w4-q14.question: In the year-end stock count, closing inventory was wrongly counted as ₹1,50,000 instead of ₹1,20,000, and the error was not caught. What is the effect on this year's profit and next year's profit?
options: This year ₹30,000 lower, next year ₹30,000 higher
This year ₹30,000 higher, no effect next year
Only the balance sheet is wrong, no effect on profit
This year ₹30,000 higher, next year ₹30,000 lower
facc-w4-q14.explanation: COGS = opening + purchases − closing. Closing 30,000 too high ⇒ this year's COGS 30,000 too low ⇒ profit ₹30,000 higher. The same closing becomes next year's opening ⇒ next year's COGS 30,000 too high ⇒ profit ₹30,000 lower. 'No effect next year' forgets that closing becomes the next opening; and closing inventory changes profit directly, not just the balance sheet.

facc-w4-q15.question: At year end (before these items) a company's PBT is ₹20,00,000. Items: (A) warranty claims ₹3,00,000 — outflow probable, estimate reliable; (B) a supplier's ₹5,00,000 claim — only possible; (C) a ₹2,50,000 tax dispute — outflow probable, but the amount cannot be reliably estimated; (D) a ₹1,00,000 case — chance remote. After applying Ind AS 37, what is PBT and how much contingent liability is disclosed in the notes?
facc-w4-q15.explanation: Only A gets a provision (probable + reliable): PBT = 20,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹17,00,000. B is possible and C cannot be measured reliably — both are contingent liabilities: 5,00,000 + 2,50,000 = ₹7,50,000. D is remote, nothing. ₹14,50,000 also provides for C, ₹8,50,000 also discloses the remote case, and ₹9,50,000 provides for A, B and C.

facc-w5-q1.question: A company's profit before tax is ₹12,00,000 and the tax rate is 25%. What is the profit after tax?
facc-w5-q1.explanation: Tax = 12,00,000 × 25% = 3,00,000; PAT = 12,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹9,00,000. ₹3,00,000 is just the tax, and ₹15,00,000 is the trap of adding the tax instead of subtracting it.

facc-w5-q2.question: Which statement about a dividend paid to equity shareholders is correct?
options: It is an expense in the P&L and reduces PAT
It becomes a liability at the start of the year
It is a distribution of profit that reduces retained earnings
facc-w5-q2.explanation: A dividend is not a cost of earning profit; it shares out profit already earned among the owners. So it is deducted from retained earnings after PAT. The first option is the most common trap — a dividend does not change PAT.

facc-w5-q3.question: A company's opening retained earnings are ₹5,00,000. This year's PAT is ₹3,00,000 and a dividend of ₹1.5 per share was paid on 80,000 equity shares. What are closing retained earnings?
facc-w5-q3.explanation: Dividend = 80,000 × 1.5 = 1,20,000. Closing = 5,00,000 + 3,00,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹6,80,000. ₹8,00,000 comes from forgetting the dividend, ₹1,80,000 from forgetting the opening balance, and ₹9,20,000 from adding the dividend.

facc-w5-q4.question: Which of these transactions does NOT change the business's **total assets**?
options: Took a new loan from the bank
facc-w5-q4.explanation: Machinery for cash: one asset (machinery) rises and another (cash) falls by the same amount — the total is unchanged. A loan and new capital raise assets; paying a creditor reduces both cash and liabilities, so total assets fall.

facc-w5-q5.question: A company's PBT is ₹10,00,000, the tax rate is 25%, and it paid a dividend of ₹3,00,000 during the year. What is the dividend payout ratio?
facc-w5-q5.explanation: PAT = 10,00,000 × 75% = 7,50,000. Payout = 3,00,000 ÷ 7,50,000 = 40%. 30% comes from dividing by PBT; 60% is the retention ratio, not the payout.

facc-w5-q6.question: A business has Assets ₹6,00,000 = Liabilities ₹2,00,000 + Equity ₹4,00,000. Then: (a) it buys inventory of ₹50,000 on credit, (b) pays a supplier ₹20,000 in cash, (c) sells inventory costing ₹30,000 for ₹45,000 cash. What are total assets now?
facc-w5-q6.explanation: (a) inventory +50,000, payables +50,000. (b) cash −20,000, payables −20,000. (c) cash +45,000, inventory −30,000, equity +15,000. Assets = 6,00,000 + 50,000 − 20,000 + 45,000 − 30,000 = ₹6,45,000 = liabilities 2,30,000 + equity 4,15,000. ₹6,75,000 comes from forgetting to remove the inventory sold; ₹6,65,000 from forgetting the cash paid to the supplier.

facc-w5-q7.question: A company's income tax expense for the year is ₹3,60,000, and it paid ₹2,80,000 of advance tax during the year. What is the current tax liability (tax payable) at year end?
facc-w5-q7.explanation: Tax payable = tax expense − advance tax = 3,60,000 − 2,80,000 = ₹80,000. ₹3,60,000 forgets the advance tax, ₹2,80,000 is what has already been paid, and ₹6,40,000 adds the two.

facc-w5-q8.question: A company paid a total dividend of ₹6,00,000 on 2,40,000 equity shares. What is the dividend per share (DPS)?
facc-w5-q8.explanation: DPS = total dividend ÷ number of shares = 6,00,000 ÷ 2,40,000 = ₹2.50. ₹0.40 comes from dividing the other way (shares ÷ dividend), ₹25.00 from misplacing the decimal, and ₹1.25 halves the answer for no reason.

facc-w5-q9.question: Under the debit-credit rules, the **increase** of which of these accounts is recorded on the debit side?
facc-w5-q9.explanation: Increases in assets and expenses are debits, so an increase in rent expense is a debit. A bank loan (liability), share capital (equity) and sales (revenue) are credited when they increase. Debiting revenue just because it is also a 'P&L item' is a common mistake.

facc-w5-q10.question: A company's PAT is ₹16,00,000. Of this, ₹12,00,000 was retained and the rest was paid as dividend to equity shareholders. The company has 4,00,000 equity shares. What are the payout ratio and DPS?
facc-w5-q10.explanation: Dividend = 16,00,000 − 12,00,000 = 4,00,000. Payout = 4,00,000 ÷ 16,00,000 = 25%; DPS = 4,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = ₹1.00. 75% / ₹3.00 treats the retained amount as dividend, ₹4.00 divides PAT by shares (that is EPS), and 33.3% divides dividend by the retained amount instead of PAT.

facc-w5-q11.question: Goods were sold to a customer on credit last month. Today the customer paid ₹25,000 in cash. What is the effect of this transaction on the accounting equation?
options: Assets and equity both rose by ₹25,000
Assets and liabilities both rose by ₹25,000
One asset rose and another fell by the same amount; total unchanged
Assets and liabilities both fell by ₹25,000
facc-w5-q11.explanation: Cash +25,000 and trade receivables −25,000 — only the form of assets changed (asset ↑ asset ↓). Revenue was already recorded on the day of sale, so equity does not rise again — the 'equity rose' option double counts the sale. Liabilities are not involved in this transaction.

facc-w5-q12.question: A company's PBT is ₹20,00,000, the tax rate is 25%, and it has 5,00,000 equity shares. During the year the board declared and paid an interim dividend of ₹1 per share. After year end (31 March) the board proposed a final dividend of ₹2 per share, to be approved later at the AGM. Opening retained earnings were ₹8,00,000. What are closing retained earnings on 31 March?
facc-w5-q12.explanation: PAT = 20,00,000 − 25% = 15,00,000. Interim dividend = 5,00,000 × ₹1 = 5,00,000. Closing RE = 8,00,000 + 15,00,000 − 5,00,000 = ₹18,00,000. A final dividend proposed after year end is not yet a liability; it is only disclosed in the notes. ₹8,00,000 also subtracts the final dividend, ₹23,00,000 forgets even the interim, and ₹13,00,000 subtracts the final instead of the interim.

facc-w5-q13.question: A company's opening tax payable was ₹40,000 (last year's, paid off this year). This year PBT is ₹12,00,000 and the tax rate is 25%. Advance tax of ₹2,50,000 was paid for this year. What is the closing tax payable at year end?
facc-w5-q13.explanation: This year's tax expense = 12,00,000 × 25% = 3,00,000. Last year's 40,000 has been paid, so it is gone. Closing payable = 3,00,000 − 2,50,000 = ₹50,000. ₹90,000 treats the opening 40,000 as still unpaid, ₹3,00,000 forgets the advance tax, and ₹10,000 subtracts the opening once more from this year's tax.

facc-w5-q14.question: At the start a company has Assets ₹50,00,000 = Liabilities ₹20,00,000 + Equity ₹30,00,000. PBT for the year is ₹8,00,000 (all received in cash). Tax rate 25%: ₹1,50,000 of it was paid as advance tax, the rest is payable at year end. A ₹2,00,000 dividend was declared and paid. What are total liabilities and equity at year end?

facc-w5-q15.question: A company's PBT is ₹24,00,000 and the tax rate is 25%. Its retention ratio is 60%, and it has 3,00,000 equity shares. What is the dividend per share?
facc-w5-q15.explanation: PAT = 24,00,000 × 75% = 18,00,000. Payout = 1 − 60% = 40% ⇒ dividend = 7,20,000. DPS = 7,20,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = ₹2.40. ₹3.60 treats retention as payout, ₹3.20 applies the payout to PBT (it should be PAT), and ₹4.80 makes both mistakes together.

facc-w6-q1.question: In a manufacturing company's balance sheet, which of these items is a **current asset**?
options: A long-term investment in another company's shares
facc-w6-q1.explanation: Inventory is sold and turned into cash within the normal operating cycle, so it is a current asset. Land and goodwill last for years, and a long-term investment is held for the long run too — all three are non-current.

facc-w6-q2.question: A company's items: inventories ₹3,00,000; trade receivables ₹2,50,000; cash ₹1,00,000; prepaid expenses ₹20,000; trade payables ₹2,80,000; short-term borrowings ₹1,20,000; long-term borrowings ₹5,00,000; PPE ₹9,00,000. What is the working capital?
facc-w6-q2.explanation: Current assets = 3,00,000 + 2,50,000 + 1,00,000 + 20,000 = 6,70,000. Current liabilities = 2,80,000 + 1,20,000 = 4,00,000. WC = ₹2,70,000. −₹2,30,000 comes from treating long-term borrowings as current too; ₹2,50,000 from leaving out prepaid expenses; ₹3,90,000 from leaving out short-term borrowings.

facc-w6-q3.question: A company issued 50,000 equity shares (face value ₹10) at ₹60 per share and received the full amount. How much goes to securities premium?
options: ₹0 — the premium becomes income in the P&L
facc-w6-q3.explanation: Premium per share = 60 − 10 = ₹50; total = 50,000 × 50 = ₹25,00,000 (other equity). Share capital = 50,000 × 10 = 5,00,000, and total cash is 30,00,000. The premium is shareholders' capital, not income — so the last option is wrong.

facc-w6-q4.question: What does the 'consolidated balance sheet' in an annual report show?
options: Only the parent company's own assets and liabilities
The total of the last five years' balance sheets
The parent and its subsidiaries combined as one group
Only the subsidiaries' figures, without the parent
facc-w6-q4.explanation: Consolidated statements combine the parent and its subsidiaries as one economic entity (removing transactions between them). The parent's own figures are in the standalone statements — the first option describes standalone.

facc-w6-q5.question: On 31 March a company has a ₹10,00,000 term loan repayable in annual instalments of ₹2,00,000; the first instalment is due within the next 12 months. How is it shown in the balance sheet?
facc-w6-q5.explanation: The part due within the next 12 months (₹2,00,000) is a current maturity — it goes in current liabilities. The remaining ₹8,00,000 is non-current borrowings. Showing the whole loan as non-current is the most common mistake, and it makes working capital look bigger.

facc-w6-q6.question: A company has total assets of ₹50,00,000, non-current liabilities of ₹15,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹9,00,000. It has 1,50,000 equity shares (face value ₹10). What is the book value per share?
facc-w6-q6.explanation: Total equity = 50,00,000 − 15,00,000 − 9,00,000 = 26,00,000 (share capital 15,00,000 + other equity 11,00,000). Book value = 26,00,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = ₹17.33. ₹33.33 is the trap of dividing total assets by shares (liabilities do not belong to owners); ₹10 is the face value; ₹7.33 is only other equity per share.

facc-w6-q7.question: In an annual report's balance sheet, what does 'capital work-in-progress' show?
options: Half-finished goods in the factory — a current asset
Money owed to employees for work done — a current liability
A factory or plant under construction, not yet in use — a non-current asset
The part of share capital still to be received
facc-w6-q7.explanation: Capital work-in-progress is unfinished construction — such as a building being built or machinery being installed — that moves into PPE once complete, so it is a non-current asset. Half-finished goods are 'work-in-progress inventory' and sit in inventories (a current asset); the similar name causes the common confusion.

facc-w6-q8.question: A company's total equity is ₹36,00,000, and it has 3,00,000 equity shares (face value ₹10). What is the book value per share?
facc-w6-q8.explanation: Book value per share = total equity ÷ shares = 36,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = ₹12. ₹10 is only the face value, ₹2 is the part above face value (reserves per share), and ₹120 comes from a misplaced zero.

facc-w6-q9.question: Which of these items will be a **current liability** in a company's balance sheet?
options: A debenture loan repayable after 10 years (no instalment in the next 12 months)
Advances from customers whose goods are to be delivered in the next 3 months
facc-w6-q9.explanation: The obligation for customer advances must be met within the next 12 months, so it is a current liability (other current liabilities). A debenture with no instalment in the next 12 months is non-current. Securities premium is other equity, and CWIP is a non-current asset.

facc-w6-q10.question: A company's equity items: equity share capital ₹10,00,000; securities premium ₹6,00,000; general reserve ₹3,00,000; retained earnings ₹5,00,000. Under Schedule III, what are 'other equity' and total equity?
facc-w6-q10.explanation: Other equity = securities premium + general reserve + retained earnings = 6,00,000 + 3,00,000 + 5,00,000 = 14,00,000. Total equity = 10,00,000 + 14,00,000 = ₹24,00,000. ₹8,00,000 leaves out the premium (it is a reserve too, not income), ₹24,00,000 counts share capital inside other equity, and ₹5,00,000 takes only retained earnings.

facc-w6-q11.question: A company: current assets ₹18,00,000; trade payables ₹6,00,000; other current liabilities ₹2,00,000; a term loan of ₹12,00,000, of which ₹3,00,000 is due in the next 12 months. What is the working capital?
facc-w6-q11.explanation: Current liabilities = 6,00,000 + 2,00,000 + 3,00,000 (current maturity of the loan) = 11,00,000. Working capital = 18,00,000 − 11,00,000 = ₹7,00,000. ₹10,00,000 leaves the current maturity in non-current, −₹2,00,000 treats the whole loan as current, and ₹12,00,000 subtracts only trade payables.

facc-w6-q12.question: A company's balance sheet items: PPE ₹30,00,000; capital work-in-progress ₹4,00,000; non-current investments ₹6,00,000; inventories ₹9,00,000; trade receivables ₹7,00,000; cash ₹3,00,000; equity share capital ₹15,00,000; other equity ?; long-term borrowings ₹10,00,000; trade payables ₹6,00,000; short-term borrowings ₹4,00,000; other current liabilities ₹2,00,000. What are other equity and working capital?
facc-w6-q12.explanation: Non-current assets = 30 + 4 + 6 = 40 lakh; current assets = 9 + 7 + 3 = 19 lakh; total = 59,00,000. Liabilities = 10,00,000 + (6 + 4 + 2 = 12 lakh) = 22,00,000. Equity = 37,00,000 ⇒ other equity = 37,00,000 − 15,00,000 = ₹22,00,000. WC = 19,00,000 − 12,00,000 = ₹7,00,000. ₹37,00,000 is total equity; WC of ₹11,00,000 leaves short-term borrowings out of current liabilities; ₹18,00,000 forgets to count CWIP in assets.

facc-w6-q13.question: A company has 2,00,000 equity shares (face value ₹10) and other equity of ₹30,00,000. It now issues 50,000 new shares at ₹70 per share and receives the full amount. What is the book value per share after the issue?
facc-w6-q13.explanation: Equity before = 20,00,000 + 30,00,000 = 50,00,000. New money = 50,000 × 70 = 35,00,000 (5,00,000 share capital + 30,00,000 securities premium). New equity = 85,00,000; shares = 2,50,000 ⇒ BVPS = ₹34.00. ₹25.00 is the value before the issue, ₹22.00 adds only face value (the premium is equity too), and ₹42.50 divides the new equity by the old number of shares.

facc-w6-q14.question: On 31 March a company has: trade payables ₹8,00,000; a 5-year term loan of ₹20,00,000 (with a ₹4,00,000 instalment due in the next 12 months); customer advances ₹1,50,000; statutory dues (GST, TDS) ₹50,000; current tax liability ₹1,00,000; debentures of ₹10,00,000 due after 3 years. What are total current liabilities?
facc-w6-q14.explanation: Current = trade payables 8,00,000 + current maturity of the loan 4,00,000 + customer advances 1,50,000 + statutory dues 50,000 + current tax 1,00,000 = ₹15,00,000. The debentures and the remaining 16,00,000 of the loan are non-current. ₹11,00,000 forgets the current maturity, ₹31,00,000 puts the whole loan in current, and ₹13,50,000 does not treat customer advances as a liability.

facc-w6-q15.question: A company's working capital is ₹5,00,000. Before year end: (i) it took a 5-year loan of ₹2,00,000 and kept the cash in the bank; (ii) it paid ₹1,00,000 of trade payables in cash; (iii) it bought a machine for ₹1,50,000 in cash. What is the working capital now?
facc-w6-q15.explanation: (i) Cash (current asset) +2,00,000, loan is non-current ⇒ WC +2,00,000. (ii) Cash −1,00,000 and payables −1,00,000 ⇒ WC unchanged. (iii) Cash −1,50,000, the machine is non-current ⇒ WC −1,50,000. New WC = 5,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 1,50,000 = ₹5,50,000. ₹4,50,000 treats paying payables as reducing WC, ₹7,00,000 forgets the cash spent on the machine, and ₹3,50,000 makes the long-term loan a current liability.

facc-w7-q1.question: A company's revenue is ₹8,00,000 and cost of goods sold is ₹4,80,000. What is the gross profit margin?
facc-w7-q1.explanation: GP = 8,00,000 − 4,80,000 = 3,20,000. Margin = 3,20,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 40%. 66.7% comes from dividing GP by COGS (that is the markup, not the margin); 60% is COGS as a share of revenue.

facc-w7-q2.question: What must be subtracted to go from EBITDA to EBIT?
facc-w7-q2.explanation: EBIT = EBITDA − D&A; the 'DA' drops out of the name itself. Finance costs are subtracted after EBIT (on the way to PBT), and tax after PBT — both are lower steps of the ladder.

facc-w7-q3.question: A company's PAT is ₹6,00,000, tax expense ₹2,00,000, finance costs ₹1,50,000 and depreciation ₹2,50,000. There is no other income or exceptional item. What is EBITDA?
facc-w7-q3.explanation: Add back from the bottom: PAT 6,00,000 + tax 2,00,000 = PBT 8,00,000; + finance 1,50,000 = EBIT 9,50,000; + depreciation 2,50,000 = EBITDA ₹12,00,000. ₹9,50,000 is EBIT (depreciation not added back) and ₹8,00,000 is only PBT.

facc-w7-q4.question: A company: revenue from operations ₹60,00,000; other income (FD interest) ₹4,00,000; total expenses ₹50,00,000, including depreciation of ₹3,00,000 and finance costs of ₹2,00,000. If EBITDA excludes other income, what is EBITDA?
facc-w7-q4.explanation: Operating expenses (without D&A and finance costs) = 50,00,000 − 3,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 45,00,000. EBITDA = 60,00,000 − 45,00,000 = ₹15,00,000. ₹19,00,000 comes from adding other income (not this question's convention), and ₹14,00,000 is PBT (64,00,000 − 50,00,000).

facc-w7-q5.question: A trading company: revenue ₹10,00,000; purchases of stock-in-trade ₹7,00,000; opening inventory ₹1,50,000; closing inventory ₹2,00,000. What is the gross profit?
facc-w7-q5.explanation: COGS = 1,50,000 + 7,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 6,50,000 (change in inventories = opening − closing = −50,000). GP = 10,00,000 − 6,50,000 = ₹3,50,000. ₹3,00,000 comes from ignoring the inventory change, and ₹2,50,000 from using the wrong sign (+50,000) for the change.

facc-w7-q6.question: A company's PAT is ₹45,00,000 and its preference dividend is ₹5,00,000. It had 8,00,000 equity shares on 1 April and issued 4,00,000 new shares on 1 October (financial year 1 April – 31 March). What is basic EPS?
facc-w7-q6.explanation: The new shares were outstanding for 6 months: weighted shares = 8,00,000 + 4,00,000 × 6/12 = 10,00,000. Profit for equity = 45,00,000 − 5,00,000 = 40,00,000. EPS = ₹4.00. ₹3.33 comes from using the 12,00,000 year-end shares, ₹4.50 from not deducting the preference dividend, ₹5.00 from using only the opening shares.

facc-w7-q7.question: A textile company received ₹2,00,000 of interest on fixed deposits. Where will this appear in the Schedule III statement of profit and loss?
facc-w7-q7.explanation: A textile company's main business is selling cloth; FD interest is side income, so it is other income. Revenue from operations is only for the main business (sales, service fees). Finance costs are interest the company pays, not interest it receives.

facc-w7-q8.question: A company's revenue from operations is ₹40,00,000 and PAT is ₹3,00,000. What is the net profit margin?
facc-w7-q8.explanation: Net profit margin = PAT ÷ revenue = 3,00,000 ÷ 40,00,000 = 7.5%. 13.33% comes from dividing the other way (revenue ÷ PAT), and 75% / 0.75% from misplacing the decimal.

facc-w7-q9.question: A company's PAT is ₹12,00,000 (tax already deducted), it has no preference shares, and 4,00,000 equity shares were outstanding for the whole year. What is the basic EPS?
facc-w7-q9.explanation: Basic EPS = PAT ÷ shares = 12,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = ₹3.00. ₹0.33 divides the other way, ₹2.25 charges 25% tax on PAT again (tax is already deducted in PAT), and ₹30.00 is a decimal error.

facc-w7-q10.question: A company's PBT is ₹14,00,000. Finance costs are ₹3,00,000, other income ₹1,00,000 and depreciation ₹2,00,000. There are no exceptional items. Using the course convention (EBIT excludes other income), what is EBIT?
facc-w7-q10.explanation: PBT = EBIT + other income − finance costs ⇒ EBIT = 14,00,000 − 1,00,000 + 3,00,000 = ₹16,00,000. ₹17,00,000 forgets to remove other income, ₹18,00,000 is EBITDA (depreciation added back too), and ₹11,00,000 subtracts finance costs instead of adding them back.

facc-w7-q11.question: A company's PAT is ₹20,00,000. Remeasurement of an employee benefit plan gave a loss of ₹1,50,000 in OCI. 10,00,000 equity shares were outstanding for the whole year, with no preference shares. What are the total comprehensive income and basic EPS?
facc-w7-q11.explanation: TCI = PAT + OCI = 20,00,000 − 1,50,000 = ₹18,50,000. EPS is based on PAT: 20,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹2.00. ₹1.85 computes EPS on TCI, ₹21,50,000 treats the OCI loss as a gain, and ₹20,00,000 ignores OCI altogether.

facc-w7-q12.question: A trading company: revenue from operations ₹80,00,000; other income ₹2,00,000; purchases of stock-in-trade ₹50,00,000; opening inventory ₹6,00,000; closing inventory ₹10,00,000; employee benefits ₹8,00,000; other expenses ₹5,00,000; depreciation ₹3,00,000; finance costs ₹2,00,000; tax rate 25%. What is PAT?
facc-w7-q12.explanation: Changes in inventories = 6,00,000 − 10,00,000 = −4,00,000 ⇒ COGS = 46,00,000. EBITDA = 80 − 46 − 8 − 5 = 21 lakh; EBIT = 18 lakh; PBT = 18 + 2 (other income) − 2 (finance costs) = 18,00,000. Tax 4,50,000 ⇒ PAT ₹13,50,000. ₹7,50,000 flips the sign of the inventory change (COGS 54 lakh), ₹12,00,000 forgets other income, and ₹18,00,000 is PBT with tax still to be deducted.

facc-w7-q13.question: A company's PAT is ₹62,00,000 and preference dividend ₹2,00,000. On 1 April there were 10,00,000 equity shares; 4,00,000 new shares were issued on 1 January (financial year 1 April – 31 March). What is basic EPS?
facc-w7-q13.explanation: Profit for equity holders = 62,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 60,00,000. The new shares were outstanding only for Jan–Mar = 3 months: weighted shares = 10,00,000 + 4,00,000 × 3/12 = 11,00,000. EPS = 60,00,000 ÷ 11,00,000 = ₹5.45. ₹4.29 uses the year-end 14,00,000 shares, ₹5.64 does not subtract the preference dividend, and ₹6.00 ignores the new shares completely.

facc-w7-q14.question: A company's revenue from operations is ₹60,00,000 and its net profit margin is 10%. Tax is 25% of PBT. Finance costs are ₹1,00,000 and depreciation ₹3,00,000; there is no other income or exceptional item. What is the EBITDA margin?
facc-w7-q14.explanation: PAT = 60,00,000 × 10% = 6,00,000. PBT = 6,00,000 ÷ 75% = 8,00,000. EBITDA = PBT + finance costs + depreciation = 8,00,000 + 1,00,000 + 3,00,000 = 12,00,000 ⇒ margin 20%. 16.67% forgets to add back tax (starts from PAT), 19.17% takes tax as 25% of PAT, and 15% is the EBIT margin (depreciation not added back).

facc-w7-q15.question: A company's profit before exceptional items and tax is ₹30,00,000. A factory fire caused an exceptional loss of ₹6,00,000. Tax is 25% of PBT. OCI shows a gain of ₹2,00,000. 6,00,000 equity shares were outstanding all year, with no preference shares. What is basic EPS?
facc-w7-q15.explanation: PBT = 30,00,000 − 6,00,000 = 24,00,000. Tax = 6,00,000 ⇒ PAT = 18,00,000. EPS = 18,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = ₹3.00 (OCI does not enter EPS). ₹3.75 ignores the exceptional loss, ₹3.33 adds the OCI gain to PAT, and ₹2.75 charges tax on the ₹30,00,000 before the exceptional item.

facc-w8-q1.question: The business paid staff a salary of ₹15,000 in cash. What is the correct journal entry?
facc-w8-q1.explanation: Salary expense rises ⇒ debit; cash (an asset) falls ⇒ credit. The first option is reversed. Capital would be debited if the owner took money for himself (drawings) — staff salary is a business expense.

facc-w8-q2.question: Which of these accounts normally has a **debit** balance?
facc-w8-q2.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's equity, so an increase in drawings is a debit and the normal balance is debit. Trade payables (liability), share capital (equity) and revenue all increase with a credit. Treating drawings as a credit like equity is the common trap.

facc-w8-q3.question: Goods were sold to Ramesh on credit last month. Today Ramesh paid ₹20,000 in cash. What is the correct entry?
facc-w8-q3.explanation: Cash (an asset) rises ⇒ debit; the receivable from Ramesh (an asset) falls ⇒ credit. Crediting Sales is the big trap — the sale was already recorded last month, and recording it again would double the revenue.

facc-w8-q4.question: The cash account has an opening balance of ₹12,000 debit. During the month receipts are ₹45,000 and ₹8,000; payments are ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹4,500. What is the cash account balance at month-end?
facc-w8-q4.explanation: Debit side = 12,000 + 45,000 + 8,000 = 65,000; credit side = 20,000 + 30,000 + 4,500 = 54,500. Balance = ₹10,500 debit (the debit side is bigger). ₹1,500 credit comes from forgetting the opening balance, and ₹15,000 from leaving out one payment (4,500).

facc-w8-q5.question: Which of these errors does **not** cause a difference in the trial balance totals?
options: Only the debit side of an entry was posted
A ledger account was totalled wrongly
₹500 was posted as the debit and ₹5,000 as the credit
The purchase of new machinery was debited to the Repairs account
facc-w8-q5.explanation: Debiting machinery to Repairs is an error of principle: debit and credit are still equal, just in the wrong type of account — the TB agrees, but profit and assets are understated. The other three errors make one side differ from the other, so the TB shows a difference.

facc-w8-q6.question: A trial balance has a debit total of ₹2,45,000 and a credit total of ₹2,52,000. Two errors are found: (a) rent of ₹3,500 was correctly credited to the cash account but never posted to the Rent account; (b) a sales return of ₹1,750 was posted to the credit side of the Sales Returns account instead of the debit side. After correcting both, what is the trial balance total?
facc-w8-q6.explanation: (a) Add the rent debit: debit 2,45,000 + 3,500 = 2,48,500. (b) Remove the sales return from the credit side and put it on the debit side: debit 2,48,500 + 1,750 = 2,50,250; credit 2,52,000 − 1,750 = 2,50,250. Both agree. ₹2,48,500 comes from fixing only the first error; ₹2,53,750 from adding the return to the credit side instead of removing it.

facc-w8-q7.question: The business bought office furniture worth ₹18,000 on credit from 'Sharma Furnishers'. What is the correct journal entry?
facc-w8-q7.explanation: Furniture, an asset, came in (debit), and money is owed to Sharma Furnishers — a liability increased (credit). The Purchases account is only for goods bought for resale, not furniture. Crediting cash is wrong because no payment has been made yet.

facc-w8-q8.question: In the traditional golden rules, what is the rule for a **real account** (assets)?
options: Debit the receiver, credit the giver
Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains
Debit what goes out, credit what comes in
facc-w8-q8.explanation: For real accounts (assets): debit what comes into the business and credit what goes out. 'Debit the receiver, credit the giver' is the rule for personal accounts, and the expenses/incomes rule is for nominal accounts. The last option reverses the real account rule.

facc-w8-q9.question: Which of these accounts normally has a **credit** balance?
facc-w8-q9.explanation: Outstanding salary is a liability, and liabilities normally have a credit balance. Rent (an expense), cash (an asset) and drawings all normally have debit balances. Drawings are linked to equity, so thinking they are a credit is a common trap.

facc-w8-q10.question: The business sold goods worth ₹50,000 to 'Verma Stores': ₹15,000 was received in cash immediately and Verma Stores will pay the rest later. What is the correct compound journal entry?
options: Dr Cash ₹15,000; Dr Verma Stores ₹35,000; Cr Sales ₹50,000
Dr Sales ₹50,000; Cr Cash ₹15,000; Cr Verma Stores ₹35,000
Dr Cash ₹15,000; Dr Verma Stores ₹35,000; Cr Purchases ₹50,000
facc-w8-q10.explanation: Cash (an asset) of 15,000 came in and 35,000 is due from Verma Stores (a receivable, an asset) — both are debits. The full 50,000 of sales revenue is credited. The second option reverses the whole entry, the third treats the full amount as cash, and the fourth credits Purchases instead of Sales.

facc-w8-q11.question: Goods worth ₹8,000 were sold to Mohan on credit, but the posting was wrongly debited to Sohan's account (Sales was correctly credited). What kind of error is this, and will the trial balance agree?
options: Error of principle; the trial balance will not agree
Error of omission; the trial balance will agree
Error of commission; the trial balance will agree
Error of commission; the trial balance will not agree
facc-w8-q11.explanation: The amount was posted to the correct side (debit), just to the wrong party's account — this is an error of commission. Debit and credit are both 8,000, so the totals stay equal and the TB does not catch it. An error of principle is a capital vs revenue mistake, and in omission the whole entry is left out.

facc-w8-q12.question: A shop's ledger balances: Cash ₹42,000; Furniture ₹60,000; Purchases ₹1,30,000; Sales ₹2,10,000; Rent ₹24,000; Trade payables ₹36,000; Trade receivables ₹55,000; Drawings ₹15,000; Salary ₹40,000; Bank loan ₹50,000; Capital ?. What must Capital be for the trial balance to agree, and what is the TB total?
facc-w8-q12.explanation: Debit balances: Cash 42,000 + Furniture 60,000 + Purchases 1,30,000 + Rent 24,000 + Receivables 55,000 + Drawings 15,000 + Salary 40,000 = 3,66,000. Credit: Sales 2,10,000 + Payables 36,000 + Loan 50,000 = 2,96,000 ⇒ Capital = ₹70,000, total ₹3,66,000. ₹40,000 puts drawings on the credit side, ₹1,70,000 puts the bank loan on the debit side, and ₹22,000 puts rent on the credit side.

facc-w8-q13.question: The supplier 'Kapoor Traders' account has an opening balance of ₹25,000 credit (we owe them). During the month: goods worth ₹60,000 were bought from them on credit; ₹40,000 was paid to them in cash; damaged goods worth ₹5,000 were returned to them (purchase return). What is the balance on Kapoor Traders' account at month end?
facc-w8-q13.explanation: Credit side: opening 25,000 + purchase 60,000 = 85,000. Debit side: payment 40,000 + return 5,000 = 45,000. Balance = ₹40,000 credit (still owed). ₹40,000 debit reverses the side, ₹50,000 treats the return as increasing the liability, and ₹10,000 works as if the opening were a debit balance.

facc-w8-q14.question: A trial balance shows a debit total of ₹4,80,000 and a credit total of ₹4,92,500. Three errors were found: (a) a ₹6,000 salary was posted to the Salary account as only ₹600 (cash was correctly credited); (b) a ₹7,100 credit sale was not posted to the customer's account at all (Sales was correctly credited); (c) a ₹2,000 furniture purchase was debited to the Purchases account. After fixing all three, what is the trial balance total?
facc-w8-q14.explanation: (a) The salary debit was 5,400 short ⇒ debit +5,400. (b) The customer's 7,100 debit was missing ⇒ debit +7,100. (c) Error of principle: moving from Purchases to Furniture, both debits — no effect on the total. Debit = 4,80,000 + 5,400 + 7,100 = 4,92,500 = credit. ₹4,93,100 adds the full 6,000, ₹4,94,500 also adds (c) to the total, and ₹4,85,400 fixes only (a).

facc-w8-q15.question: A new business's transactions for the month: (1) ₹3,00,000 capital deposited in the bank; (2) goods worth ₹1,20,000 bought on credit from 'Anand Traders'; (3) goods worth ₹1,40,000 sold on credit to 'Neha Retail'; (4) ₹1,00,000 received from Neha in the bank; (5) ₹70,000 paid to Anand from the bank; (6) ₹12,000 electricity bill paid from the bank. After balancing the accounts, what is the trial balance total?
facc-w8-q15.explanation: Bank = 3,00,000 + 1,00,000 − 70,000 − 12,000 = 3,18,000 Dr. Debit: Bank 3,18,000 + Purchases 1,20,000 + Neha 40,000 + Electricity 12,000 = 4,90,000. Credit: Capital 3,00,000 + Anand 50,000 + Sales 1,40,000 = 4,90,000. ₹5,90,000 credits Neha's receipt to Sales (revenue counted twice); ₹5,60,000 does not balance Anand's account (writes the gross 1,20,000 and 70,000 separately); ₹6,60,000 balances neither Neha nor Anand.

facc-w9-q1.question: In the indirect method, why is depreciation added back to profit?
options: It is a non-cash expense — it reduced profit but no cash left the business this year
Depreciation brings cash into the company
To make the tax expense look smaller
facc-w9-q1.explanation: The cash for the machine left when it was bought (under investing); depreciation only spreads that cost over the years. It reduced profit without moving cash, so it is added back. It is not a source of cash — that is the most common misunderstanding.

facc-w9-q2.question: During the year trade receivables rose from ₹2,00,000 to ₹2,80,000. When computing CFO by the indirect method, what do you do with this?
options: Ignore it, it is a balance sheet item
facc-w9-q2.explanation: Higher receivables mean some sales are in profit but their cash has not arrived. So subtract the ₹80,000 increase. You would add it if receivables fell (old dues being collected).

facc-w9-q3.question: A proprietorship (ignore tax) has net profit of ₹2,00,000. Depreciation ₹40,000; inventory rose by ₹30,000; trade payables rose by ₹20,000; trade receivables rose by ₹25,000. What is cash from operating activities?
facc-w9-q3.explanation: 2,00,000 + 40,000 − 30,000 (inventory ↑) + 20,000 (payables ↑) − 25,000 (receivables ↑) = ₹2,05,000. ₹2,75,000 comes from reversing the working capital signs, ₹1,25,000 from subtracting depreciation, and ₹2,40,000 from ignoring working capital.

facc-w9-q4.question: A company sold old equipment for ₹65,000; its carrying amount was ₹50,000, so a ₹15,000 gain appeared in the P&L. What is the correct treatment in the cash flow statement?
options: Add ₹15,000 in CFO, because cash came in
Subtract ₹15,000 in CFO; show the full ₹65,000 as an inflow under investing activities
facc-w9-q4.explanation: Selling equipment is an investing activity, so the full ₹65,000 of cash goes under investing. The ₹15,000 gain is already in profit — subtract it in CFO, or it gets counted twice. Ignoring the gain is exactly that double-counting trap.

facc-w9-q5.question: A company's tax expense for the year is ₹1,50,000. Its tax payable had an opening balance of ₹40,000 and a closing balance of ₹55,000. How much income tax was paid in cash during the year?
facc-w9-q5.explanation: Tax paid = opening 40,000 + expense 1,50,000 − closing 55,000 = ₹1,35,000. The payable rose, meaning not all of the expense has been paid yet. ₹1,65,000 comes from swapping opening and closing; ₹1,50,000 from assuming the expense was all paid.

facc-w9-q6.question: A company: PBT ₹8,00,000; depreciation ₹1,20,000; finance costs ₹50,000; interest income ₹20,000; trade receivables rose by ₹70,000; inventory fell by ₹30,000; trade payables fell by ₹40,000; income tax paid ₹1,80,000. Using the course convention (interest paid in financing, interest received in investing), what is CFO?
facc-w9-q6.explanation: 8,00,000 + 1,20,000 + 50,000 − 20,000 = 9,50,000. WC: −70,000 + 30,000 − 40,000 = −80,000 ⇒ 8,70,000. Tax: − 1,80,000 ⇒ ₹6,90,000. ₹8,70,000 comes from forgetting tax, ₹7,70,000 from adding the fall in payables (it should be subtracted), and ₹6,60,000 from not adjusting finance costs and interest income.

facc-w9-q7.question: Which of these cash flows of a manufacturing company is an **operating activity**?
options: Payment for buying a new machine
Payment to suppliers for raw material
Taking a new term loan from a bank
facc-w9-q7.explanation: Paying suppliers is part of running the main business, so it is operating. Buying a machine is investing (a long-term asset), and taking a loan or paying dividend is financing (dealings with owners and lenders). Putting dividend in operating as a 'regular expense' is a common mistake.

facc-w9-q8.question: During the year a company's inventory fell from ₹1,50,000 to ₹1,10,000. When working out CFO by the indirect method, what do we do with this?
options: Ignore it, it is a balance sheet item
facc-w9-q8.explanation: Inventory (a current operating asset) fell, meaning old stock was sold and cash was not tied up in it — so add ₹40,000. A change in an asset takes the opposite sign: if it rises subtract, if it falls add. Only the change is adjusted, not the closing balance (₹1,10,000).

facc-w9-q9.question: Under Ind AS 7, what is included in 'cash and cash equivalents'?
options: Cash, bank balances and all trade receivables
Cash, bank balances and highly liquid investments of up to 3 months
Cash, bank balances and 5-year fixed deposits
facc-w9-q9.explanation: Cash and cash equivalents = cash, bank balances, and highly liquid investments that turn into cash within 3 months. Receivables are not cash yet (the customer has not paid), and a 5-year FD is a long investment, not a cash equivalent. Taking only cash in hand makes the definition far too narrow.

facc-w9-q10.question: A proprietorship (ignore tax) has a net profit of ₹3,50,000. Depreciation ₹60,000; loss on sale of furniture ₹8,000; prepaid expenses rose by ₹5,000; outstanding expenses rose by ₹12,000; trade receivables fell by ₹30,000. What is the cash from operating activities?
facc-w9-q10.explanation: Adjustments: 3,50,000 + 60,000 + 8,000 (add back the loss) = 4,18,000. WC: prepaid rose −5,000; outstanding rose +12,000; receivables fell +30,000 ⇒ +37,000. CFO = ₹4,55,000. ₹4,39,000 subtracts the loss (as if it were a gain), ₹3,81,000 flips every working capital sign, and ₹3,95,000 forgets to add back depreciation.

facc-w9-q11.question: A company's tax expense for the year is ₹2,40,000. Tax payable had an opening balance of ₹65,000 and a closing balance of ₹30,000. How much income tax was paid in cash during the year?
facc-w9-q11.explanation: Tax paid = opening payable + tax expense − closing payable = 65,000 + 2,40,000 − 30,000 = ₹2,75,000. Payable fell, so the company paid more than the expense. ₹2,05,000 swaps opening and closing, ₹2,40,000 assumes the expense was paid, and ₹35,000 is only the change in payable.

facc-w9-q12.question: A company: PBT ₹12,00,000; depreciation ₹2,00,000; gain on sale of investment ₹50,000; dividend income ₹30,000; finance costs ₹80,000; trade receivables rose by ₹1,00,000; inventory rose by ₹60,000; trade payables rose by ₹90,000; customer advances fell by ₹20,000. Tax expense ₹3,00,000; tax payable opening ₹40,000, closing ₹60,000. Using the course convention, what is CFO?

facc-w9-q13.question: Work out CFO by the direct method. All sales are on credit: revenue ₹20,00,000; trade receivables opening ₹3,00,000, closing ₹3,80,000. All purchases are on credit: purchases ₹12,00,000; trade payables opening ₹1,50,000, closing ₹2,10,000. Operating expenses of ₹3,00,000 were paid in cash, and income tax of ₹1,00,000 was paid. What is the net cash from operating activities?
facc-w9-q13.explanation: Cash from customers = 20,00,000 + 3,00,000 − 3,80,000 = 19,20,000. Cash to suppliers = 12,00,000 + 1,50,000 − 2,10,000 = 11,40,000. CFO = 19,20,000 − 11,40,000 − 3,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹3,80,000. ₹5,40,000 reverses the change in receivables, ₹2,60,000 the change in payables, and ₹4,00,000 treats revenue and purchases as if they were cash.

facc-w9-q14.question: A company's net cash from operating activities is ₹7,50,000. Indirect method items: depreciation ₹1,50,000; finance costs ₹60,000; interest income ₹40,000; inventory rose by ₹80,000; trade payables rose by ₹50,000; income tax paid ₹2,00,000. Using the course convention, what was the company's PBT?
facc-w9-q14.explanation: CFO = PBT + 1,50,000 + 60,000 − 40,000 − 80,000 + 50,000 − 2,00,000 = PBT − 60,000. So PBT = 7,50,000 + 60,000 = ₹8,10,000. ₹6,90,000 applies the net adjustment the wrong way, ₹6,50,000 adds the rise in inventory, and ₹8,50,000 flips the signs of finance costs and interest income.

facc-w9-q15.question: A fast-growing firm (ignore tax) has a net profit of ₹6,00,000. Depreciation ₹1,00,000; trade receivables rose by ₹5,50,000; inventory rose by ₹3,00,000; trade payables rose by ₹1,00,000. What is CFO?
facc-w9-q15.explanation: 6,00,000 + 1,00,000 − 5,50,000 − 3,00,000 + 1,00,000 = −₹50,000. Despite the profit, cash went out because money got stuck in receivables and inventory — profit ≠ cash. −₹1,50,000 does not add back depreciation, −₹2,50,000 subtracts the rise in payables, and ₹14,50,000 flips every working capital sign.

facc-w10-q1.question: A manufacturing company paid a dividend of ₹5,00,000 in cash to its shareholders. Where does this appear in the cash flow statement?
options: Nowhere, because it is not a P&L item
facc-w10-q1.explanation: A dividend is a return to owners, so it is a financing outflow. It is not in the P&L, but cash did leave — so it must appear in the cash flow statement. The operating trap comes from linking dividends with profit.

facc-w10-q2.question: A company bought shares of another company for ₹8,00,000 as a long-term investment. Which activity does this cash flow belong to?
options: It does not appear in the cash flow statement
facc-w10-q2.explanation: Buying another company's shares is an investment ⇒ an investing outflow. It would be financing if the company issued or bought back its **own** shares — that is the most common confusion.

facc-w10-q3.question: During the year a company: received ₹5,00,000 from issuing new shares; took a new loan of ₹2,00,000; repaid an old loan of ₹3,00,000; paid dividends of ₹1,20,000; paid interest of ₹60,000. Keeping interest paid in financing, what is net cash from financing activities?
facc-w10-q3.explanation: 5,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 3,00,000 − 1,20,000 − 60,000 = ₹2,20,000. ₹2,80,000 comes from putting interest in operating, ₹3,40,000 from leaving out the dividend, and ₹11,80,000 from adding every amount (treating outflows as plus).

facc-w10-q4.question: A company's CFO is ₹4,20,000, CFI is −₹6,50,000 and CFF is ₹1,80,000. Opening cash and cash equivalents were ₹1,10,000. What are closing cash and cash equivalents?
facc-w10-q4.explanation: Net change = 4,20,000 − 6,50,000 + 1,80,000 = −50,000. Closing = 1,10,000 − 50,000 = ₹60,000. −₹50,000 is only the net change (opening balance forgotten), ₹1,60,000 comes from reversing the sign of the net change, and ₹13,60,000 from treating CFI as positive.

facc-w10-q5.question: A company's CFO is ₹9,00,000. During the year it spent ₹5,50,000 on PPE, received ₹50,000 from selling old assets, and paid a dividend of ₹1,00,000. Using the definition FCF = CFO − capital expenditure, what is free cash flow?
facc-w10-q5.explanation: By the definition, subtract only capex: 9,00,000 − 5,50,000 = ₹3,50,000. ₹4,00,000 comes from netting asset sale proceeds against capex (a different definition), and ₹2,50,000 from also subtracting the dividend — a dividend is a use of FCF, it does not reduce FCF.

facc-w10-q6.question: A company's opening net PPE is ₹20,00,000 and closing net PPE is ₹23,00,000. Depreciation for the year was ₹2,50,000. An asset with a carrying amount of ₹1,00,000 was sold for ₹70,000 cash. If there are no other investing items, what is net cash from investing activities?
facc-w10-q6.explanation: Purchases = 23,00,000 − 20,00,000 + 2,50,000 + 1,00,000 = 6,50,000. CFI = −6,50,000 + 70,000 = −₹5,80,000. −₹6,50,000 comes from forgetting the sale proceeds, −₹3,00,000 from using only the net change in PPE, and −₹5,50,000 from treating the carrying amount (1,00,000) as the cash inflow.

facc-w10-q7.question: A company took a 5-year term loan of ₹10,00,000 from a bank. Where will this appear in the cash flow statement?
options: Nowhere, because it is a liability
facc-w10-q7.explanation: Taking a loan is a cash flow with lenders, so it is a financing inflow. Investing is for long-term assets — if the loan is used to buy an asset, that is a separate investing outflow. 'It is a liability so it is nowhere' is wrong: cash actually came in.

facc-w10-q8.question: A company issued its own shares to a seller in exchange for a ₹50,00,000 building; no cash was paid. How is this treated in the cash flow statement?
options: Investing outflow of ₹50,00,000 and financing inflow of ₹50,00,000
In no activity; disclosed in the notes as a non-cash transaction
facc-w10-q8.explanation: No cash moved, so it does not appear in any activity of the cash flow statement; it is disclosed in the notes as a non-cash transaction. Showing it in both investing and financing creates a cash flow that never happened.

facc-w10-q9.question: A manufacturing company received ₹40,000 of interest on a fixed deposit. Under the course convention (Ind AS 7, non-financial company), in which activity does this appear?
options: It does not appear in the cash flow statement
facc-w10-q9.explanation: Non-financial companies show interest and dividend received under investing — it is a return on investments. Interest paid goes to financing, so the 'financing' option mixes up paid and received. This is also why interest income is subtracted from CFO under the indirect method.

facc-w10-q10.question: A company's items for the year: machinery bought ₹7,00,000; an old vehicle sold for ₹1,20,000 cash (carrying amount ₹90,000); shares of another company bought for ₹2,00,000; dividend received ₹30,000; FD interest received ₹20,000. What is the net cash from investing activities?
facc-w10-q10.explanation: CFI = −7,00,000 + 1,20,000 − 2,00,000 + 30,000 + 20,000 = −₹7,30,000.
